nameStory: This climbing vine earned its 'morning-glory' name from its spectacular funnel-shaped flowers that unfold with the first light of dawn, putting on their most dazzling display in the early morning hours. By afternoon, these same blooms often close up or fade, making morning the prime time to witness their full glory.
description: Common morning-glory is a fast-growing annual vine that can climb 6-10 feet in a single growing season. It produces heart-shaped leaves and showy trumpet-shaped flowers that come in purple, pink, blue, or white. This twining vine wraps itself around fences, poles, and other plants as it scrambles upward, creating cascades of colorful blooms from summer through fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Trumpet or funnel-shaped blooms about 2-3 inches across with five petals fused together, typically purple but can be pink, blue, or white. The flowers feel papery-thin and delicate to touch, opening early in the morning and often closing by mid-afternoon.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with a smooth, slightly fuzzy surface that feel soft between your fingers. The leaves alternate along the stem and have three distinct lobes or points, giving them an almost ivy-like appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A twining vine that spirals counter-clockwise around supports, with stems that feel slightly hairy and can grow surprisingly quickly. You can often see the vine literally wrapping itself in tight coils around fence wires or plant stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, papery seed capsules about the size of a pea that turn brown and split open to reveal 4-6 dark, triangular seeds. The capsules make a subtle rattling sound when shaken once they're fully dry.

habitat: Common morning-glory thrives in disturbed soils, garden edges, roadsides, and fence lines throughout New England. It prefers full sun and well-drained soil but is quite adaptable to various conditions. You'll often spot it climbing on chain-link fences, mailbox posts, and garden trellises in suburban and rural areas.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up. Young seedlings emerge with their characteristic heart-shaped leaves and begin their rapid climbing growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with flowers opening fresh each morning from July through August. The vine reaches its full height and produces the most abundant flowers during the longest, warmest days.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming into early fall until first frost. Seed capsules mature and turn brown, releasing seeds that will overwinter in the soil for next year's growth.
seasonality.winter: The entire plant dies back completely after frost, leaving only dried stems and scattered seeds. Nothing visible remains above ground during winter months.

funFact: Morning-glory flowers are nature's living clock - they open so predictably at dawn that Carl Linnaeus included them in his famous 'flower clock' garden, where he arranged plants that bloomed at different times to tell time throughout the day without a watch!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with field bindweed, which has smaller white or pink flowers and arrow-shaped rather than heart-shaped leaves. Remember: morning-glory has big heart-shaped leaves and large trumpet flowers, while bindweed has smaller, more pointed leaves and smaller funnel flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common' morning-glory, this species is actually native to Mexico and Central America, not New England. It's been so widely cultivated in gardens that it has naturalized and now grows wild throughout the region, sometimes becoming quite weedy in favorable conditions.
compareHints: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory. White morning-glory produces much smaller flowers and has more oval leaves, while wild potato vine has enormous heart-shaped leaves but pure white flowers that open at night rather than in the morning.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.
Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves.

Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red.
Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate.
Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers.
Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers.

Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers.

White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory.
